title: Thirteen DCU tasks report the identical 0.005439 ms for both arms at the default shape, so the paired assay cannot discriminate there
compiler_revision_id: open-cake-ir@0970a36e, open-cake-ir@4278caf2 and open-cake-ir@5151954e -- this record aggregates twenty-seven campaigns that ran at three Compiler revisions, so no single commit is its source; each row of findings/data/2026-09-18-dcu-confirmatory-medians.json names the one its campaign ran at
executor_revision: gfx938@5151954e, gfx938@0970a36e and gfx938@4278caf2 -- the same three, per row; the Executor is built from the same checkout as the Compiler here

evidence.retained: bw1100 campaign evidence for the thirteen tasks whose confirmatory receipts carry the same pooled median for both arms -- absmax_rescale, cosine_similarity, layernorm, layernorm_backward_input, residual_rmsnorm, rmsnorm, rmsnorm_input_gradient, selu, silu, softmax, softmax_backward, softplus_gradient and softsign -- together with the fourteen runs that separated. The two groups cover twenty-seven qualified tasks, which is all of them (F-2026-09-18-003). Tasks, not runs: thirty runs reached a qualified endpoint and three tasks qualified twice, so the table holds one row per task and the data file states both numbers rather than letting one word carry them. The medians are retained at findings/data/2026-09-18-dcu-confirmatory-medians.json, one row per task, each row naming the workspace and the content-addressed receipt it was read from so a reader with the host can check a single row rather than the file as a whole. The numbers in this record, in F-2026-09-18-005 and in the index are checked against that file by tests/contracts/test_dcu_medians_counts.py, by association rather than by membership: a decimal unique to one task -- a median, a ratio, or a footprint derived from that task's own Workload Contract -- must have that task named beside it, so swapping two legal values fails. Counts are checked against the group they count, and a retracted value is admitted only in a sentence that marks it as retracted. Two earlier versions claimed more than they did: one examined fifteen chosen phrases, and seven numbers could be changed across two records without failing it; the next checked membership only, so any permutation of legal values passed. F-2026-09-18-003 is scoped rather than covered -- its turn-budget counts come from its own sweep ledgers, which this table does not hold, and only its claims about this table and its stamp are checked.

the stamp on this record was open-cake-ir@3fa16b8f, a commit no campaign in the table ran at, and one the 4278caf2 campaigns postdate. A single stamp cannot name the source of an aggregate over three revisions, and writing one anyway is what ADR 0065 makes the stamp to prevent: a retained campaign has to be replayable against the tools that produced it, which is a per-campaign fact. It is now recorded per row and the field names all three

the timer's grid, derived from the retained medians rather than declared: the twenty-one distinct pooled medians in this collection are every one of them an exact multiple of 160 ns, offset by a constant 159 ns -- the greatest common divisor of all their pairwise differences is 160 ns and they share a single residue. The thirteen at the floor are all the same multiple. hip_benchmark.py's own resolution_us reports the smallest non-zero step a cohort showed, and its docstring says a short kernel's spread is largely the timer's quantum; this is that quantum measured across the whole collection

what the sweep predicts for the pair this record used to rest on, which is why that argument is withdrawn: 1.00 MiB reads 2.559 us and 1.50 MiB reads 2.719 us, a difference of 0.160 us -- exactly one quantum. silu at 1.000 MiB and softmax_backward at 1.500 MiB should therefore differ by about one grid step, and two readings one step apart collapsing into the same bucket is what a quantized timer does rather than evidence against bandwidth-bound behaviour

observation:
Thirteen operators of different arithmetic report the identical pooled median, to six decimal places, for both arms. Every task in the group reads 0.005439 ms, and the two groups together cover every qualified task.

What this record first said about why is wrong, and the correction is the substantial part. It argued from bytes: silu moves 1.000 MiB and softmax_backward 1.500, half again as much, both take 0.005439 ms, and bandwidth-bound work does not do that. That inference does not survive the record's own footprint sweep. The sweep reads 2.559 us at 1.00 MiB and 2.719 us at 1.50 MiB, so the difference it predicts for exactly that pair is 0.160 us. The assay's timer is quantized at 160 ns -- the twenty-one distinct medians here are every one an exact multiple of it -- so the predicted difference is one grid step, and two kernels one step apart reading the same value is what quantization does. The pair carried no weight, and neither does 'the task shapes sit in the flat region': at 1.000 and 1.500 MiB they sit above the plateau, in the part of the sweep that already tracks bytes.

What stands is narrower and still worth recording. Thirteen tasks land on one value, which is 33 grid steps above the constant 159 ns offset every reading here carries, and a paired comparison between two arms that both land there cannot resolve anything smaller than a step. At these footprints the byte-dependent part of the cost is about one step, so close_null at the default shape says the assay could not tell rather than that the arms matched -- which is the operational conclusion this record exists for, and it does not need the bytes argument. What is not established is why these kernels cost 5.439 us when the sweep's synthetic copy kernel reads 2.559 us at 1.00 MiB; that gap is unexplained here.

Three counts in this record have been wrong, and the corrections belong in it rather than in a later record. The floor count was asserted as seven, then as eleven; the enumeration behind the eleven listed seven tasks and then four more with selu named in both, a union of ten. Separately it said that only three runs rose above the floor and that all three showed the candidate losing. Recounting from the collected medians rather than from the previous sentence gives fourteen separated, and three of those candidates beat their baseline by more than the declared 1.05 materiality (F-2026-09-18-005). Every one of the three was arithmetic about a table, edited from the preceding sentence instead of redone.

The floor count then stood at twelve, over the twenty-six runs whose medians had been collected, with softsign qualified but absent because the host was unreachable. Its receipt has since been read: both arms 0.005439, so it is at the floor. The count is thirteen and the two groups now cover all twenty-seven qualified tasks. Thirteen plus fourteen is that twenty-seven, with nothing left over and no task unaccounted for between this record and F-2026-09-18-003. Thirteen is the fourth value this count has taken and the third time it has moved -- seven, eleven, twelve, thirteen, which is what git shows for this record -- and the first move that came from a measurement arriving rather than from a count being redone.

What the separated runs establish is the useful half: the assay resolves this hardware when the kernels cost enough steps to be resolved. The floor is what these particular kernels cost at this footprint, not the assay declining to resolve anything.

The partition rule is stated in the evidence because it decides the counts and an earlier reading of this record could not recover it: both arms on 0.005439 is 'at the floor', anything else is 'separated'. One arm on the floor therefore separates, which puts prelu and swiglu in the same group by the same rule rather than in different ones, and both are named in the fourteen.

One more correction belongs here because it is the same failure in a different field. This record was stamped open-cake-ir@3fa16b8f, and no campaign it cites ran at that commit; the nine campaigns at 4278caf2 ran after it. That was the third wrong value this field has carried, after 9b51e3cd and f91a862a, across five committed states. The campaigns ran at three revisions -- 5151954e, 0970a36e and 4278caf2 -- and a field holding one commit cannot say that, so it now names all three and each row of the medians file carries the revision its own campaign ran at.
proposed_change:
Run the DCU tasks at a footprint where the byte-dependent part of the cost is many grid steps rather than one. The sweep already says where: 1.00 MiB and 1.50 MiB are one step apart, while 1.00 MiB and 8.00 MiB are 2.559 us against 6.719 us, twenty-six steps. A shape in that range is what makes a paired comparison able to resolve a real difference, and choosing it needs no Compiler or Lab change -- create_task already takes rows and columns. Record the shape with the measurement that justified it rather than inheriting the CUDA defaults.

Do not read the thirteen close_null results as evidence that the authored candidates matched their baselines. They are evidence that the assay could not tell at a granularity of 160 ns, which is a different statement and the one the receipts support. A campaign at a shape whose differences are one step wide spends provider budget to learn nothing about latency, and that is worth knowing before a sweep rather than after.

Read resolution_us, and prefer the grid derived across a collection to a single cohort's smallest step. hip_benchmark.py computes resolution_us per cohort from the samples that cohort happened to show; taken over twenty-one distinct medians the grid is unambiguous, and it is the number that decides whether a shape can be measured at all.

This says nothing about correctness: all thirteen passed their five validation cases against the external oracle, and that half of the evaluation is unaffected by the grid. The numbers in the paragraphs above are checked against the retained medians by a test, each against the task it belongs to, because three of them were wrong while they were prose and nothing looked at them.
